name: Temazepam
lead: Temazepam is a short-to-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic prescribed for short-term treatment of insomnia. It enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation, and is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[1][2]
Grokipedia reports it was synthesised in the 1960s and marketed internationally from the 1970s.[1] It has no appearance indication and no studies of appearance outcomes.

paras: The label indicates temazepam for short-term insomnia, and guidance typically limits use to roughly seven to ten days.[1][2] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline reviewed it among drugs for chronic insomnia.[3]

Reported effects include drowsiness, dizziness, anterograde amnesia and next-day hangover effects; combination with opioids, alcohol or other CNS depressants raises the risk of respiratory depression, coma or death.[1][2] A case-cohort study of US veterans on opioid analgesics examined benzodiazepine prescribing and overdose deaths.[5] Tolerance, dependence and withdrawal can follow prolonged use, and older adults show increased sensitivity.[1][7] It is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

A randomised trial compared behavioural and pharmacological therapy, including temazepam, for late-life insomnia.[4] Registered trials have examined temazepam at high altitude and in insomnia among people with HIV.[8][9] A matched cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality; observational designs cannot show causation.[6] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

card.summary: A prescription benzodiazepine sleeping pill; sleep research only, no appearance data.
card.note: Schedule IV; dependence risk, dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

quick.overview:
Temazepam is a prescription benzodiazepine used for short-term insomnia.

No research links it to appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at GABA-A receptors, causing sedation.
quick.risks: Reported risks include drowsiness, amnesia, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, and serious respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol. Schedule IV in the US.
